questions.stem: How does Rule 6 define a safe speed?
options: A fixed maximum speed set for each size of vessel
Able to act effectively and stop in a suitable distance
Half of the vessel's full speed in the conditions
The speed posted for the nearest harbour
questions.explanation: Rule 6 gives no number. It defines safe speed by what it allows: effective action to avoid collision and stopping within a distance appropriate to the circumstances and conditions.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of the factors Rule 6 lists for every vessel when determining safe speed?
options: The colour of the vessel's hull
The size of the crew's wages
The state of visibility
The vessel's registered port
questions.explanation: The state of visibility is the first factor on the list. The other options have nothing to do with the vessel's ability to avoid collision or stop.

questions.stem: Your radar shows a clear screen in rain and sea clutter on a long range scale. You are tempted to increase speed because "nothing is out there." What does Rule 6 say that argues against this?
options: Radar can only be relied on in clear weather
Radar may miss small craft and ice, more so in weather
Radar data is only valid if the range scale is set to the shortest range
A vessel with radar must always reduce speed to half
questions.explanation: Rule 6 lists radar limits among the factors for vessels with working radar, including the effect of sea state and weather on detection and the chance that small vessels, ice and floating objects are missed. A blank screen therefore does not prove the water is clear.

questions.stem: Two vessels transit the same clear, empty channel at the same speed. One is a small, quick-turning workboat. The other is a heavily loaded vessel that takes a long distance to stop. Which statement fits Rule 6?
options: Both have the same safe speed, because conditions are the same
The loaded vessel's may be lower: manoeuvrability counts
The workboat's safe speed must be lower, because she is smaller
Safe speed applies only to the vessel with radar
questions.explanation: Safe speed is judged for each vessel. Manoeuvrability, with special reference to stopping distance and turning ability, differs between the two, so the vessel that needs more distance to stop may need to go slower in the same conditions.

questions.stem: You are in a Canadian harbour approaching a dredge at work, and you cannot tell with certainty whether your wake will adversely affect her. What does the Canadian addition to Rule 6 call for?
options: Pass at your normal cruising speed, since the dredge shows lights
Stop completely and wait for the dredge to finish
Caution, at the minimum speed that keeps you on course
Pass as close as possible to keep the passing time short
questions.explanation: The Canadian paragraphs require a caution and a speed that will not adversely affect a dredge, tow, grounded vessel or wreck. Where that cannot be determined with certainty, the passing vessel proceeds with caution at the minimum speed at which she can be kept on her course. Nothing requires stopping, and a close, fast pass is the opposite of the intent.

questions.stem: At night you are approaching a city waterfront with bright shore lights behind the anchorage. Why does Rule 6 ask you to consider this when setting your speed?
options: Background light can hide other vessels' lights
Shore lights mean you are in a harbour, where the speed limit is always 5 knots
Bright lights improve visibility, so you may safely go faster
It only matters by day
questions.explanation: Rule 6 lists, at night, the presence of background light such as from shore lights or back-scatter of your own lights. Other vessels' lights can be lost against that background, so you may detect them later and need more time. Rule 6 sets no fixed speed limit, and background light is a night-time factor.

questions.stem: Under the Canadian addition to Rule 6, in a Canadian harbour, river or inland waterway, how must you pass a tow, a grounded vessel or a wreck?
options: Any speed, 50 m off
With caution, at a speed that won't affect them
At full speed, to keep the time spent passing as short as possible
Only after receiving permission from the vessel being passed
questions.explanation: The Canadian paragraphs require caution and a speed that will not adversely affect the vessel or work being passed, mainly because of wash and wake, and compliance with any relevant notices. No fixed passing distance is given, speeding past increases wake, and the rule does not require permission from the other vessel.

questions.stem: Which of these is one of the extra factors Rule 6 lists only for vessels with operational radar?
options: The vessel's draught in relation to the available depth of water
The state of wind, sea and current
Any constraints imposed by the radar range scale in use
Traffic density, including concentrations of fishing vessels
questions.explanation: The radar factors include the radar's characteristics and limits, the constraints of the range scale in use, interference from sea state and weather, small targets that may not be detected, the number, location and movement of detected vessels, and a more exact assessment of visibility. Draught, wind, sea and current, and traffic density are factors for every vessel, with or without radar.
